modules.title: Start with your goals and care team
objectives: Choose a learning route that matches your situation
Name the people on your care team and the person you choose to support you
Explain the difference between learning online and being trained to do a treatment
modules.everydayPicture: Think of kidney care as a long jeepney route with many stops: check-ups, laboratory tests, medicine changes, maybe dialysis or a transplant one day. You do not have to know the whole route on the first day. You only need to know where you are getting on, who the driver and conductor are, and what to do if the jeepney breaks down. This first module helps you find your stop and meet the people who ride with you.

lessons.title: Your starting point
lessons.body: You can begin here whether you heard the words "kidney disease" last week or have been on dialysis for years. Pick the path that sounds most like you today: kidney disease before dialysis, hemodialysis in a unit, peritoneal dialysis (PD) at home, preparing for or living with a transplant, or supportive care without dialysis. Care partners have their own path. You may change your path at any time, and nothing here decides your treatment. Before you start, write one thing you want to be able to do with more confidence, such as "read my laboratory results without panicking" or "travel to my province for a fiesta without missing care." A clear goal makes every later lesson more useful.

lessons.title: People who can help
lessons.body: Kidney care is a team sport. Your nephrologist (kidney doctor) leads the medical plan. Nurses teach, assess and watch for problems. A pharmacist can untangle medicine lists. A dietitian turns food advice into meals you actually eat. A social worker or benefits coordinator helps with costs, PhilHealth paperwork and transport. A care partner is someone you choose to help you: a spouse, child, sibling, friend or paid helper. Choosing a care partner does not hand them your decisions. You decide what they help with and what they may know. Ask your unit or clinic for a contact card that says who answers medicine, food, treatment and money questions, and how to reach them after hours.

lessons.title: Learning at your pace
lessons.body: Each module takes about 15 minutes: five minutes of reading, five minutes of practice, and five minutes explaining it back in your own words. That last step, called teach-back, is not a test of intelligence. It is the most reliable way to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a mistake. If reading, hearing, eyesight or language makes learning hard, say so; an educator can read with you or check your answers out loud. One boundary matters from day one: finishing this course records that you learned. It does not authorize you to perform dialysis or any procedure. Hands-on training happens with your treatment team, who watch you practice and decide when you are ready.

realSituation.title: Mang Ramon finds his stop
realSituation.body: Mang Ramon, 58, drives a tricycle in Malolos and was told at a barangay screening that his kidneys were "weak." His daughter Liza, a call-center agent, opens the course on her phone. They argue: Ramon thinks he must read every module tonight, and Liza wants to start with dialysis because a neighbor is on it.
realSituation.debrief: Ramon does not need all 32 modules, and he is not on dialysis. He chooses "kidney disease before dialysis," writes his goal ("keep driving and understand my results"), and names Liza as his care partner for appointments only. He keeps the right to decide about his medicines himself. Liza learns which lessons fit her role. One choice of path, one written goal and one clear role saves both of them hours of worry.

whatResearchShows.text: Patient education works best when it is matched to what the person needs now and checked with teach-back. A systematic review of teach-back in kidney disease (6 studies, 520 participants) found improvements in knowledge, self-management and confidence, although the studies were small and varied. The 2024 KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) guideline also recommends structured education and shared care for people with chronic kidney disease.

modules.title: Understand kidney disease and your test results
objectives: Describe in plain words what healthy kidneys do
Tell the difference between eGFR and urine albumin and why both matter
Prepare one question about the trend in your results
modules.everydayPicture: Imagine your kidneys as the water-treatment plant of your body. They filter the entire liquid part of your blood about 60 times a day, roughly once every 25 minutes. They keep what you need, release what you do not, and fine-tune the water, salt and minerals so your heart, bones and brain can work. The picture breaks down in one important way: a treatment plant has alarms, but kidneys usually fail quietly. Most people feel normal until a great deal of function is gone, which is why tests, not symptoms, tell the early story.

lessons.title: What kidneys do
lessons.body: Each kidney holds about a million tiny filters called nephrons. Blood enters each filter under pressure; water and small waste molecules pass through, and the tubule that follows reclaims almost all of the water, salt and sugar the body still needs. What remains becomes urine. Kidneys also help control blood pressure, keep blood from becoming too acidic, activate vitamin D for strong bones, and make a hormone (erythropoietin) that tells the bone marrow to produce red blood cells. That is why kidney disease can show up as high blood pressure, weak bones, tiredness from anemia or swelling, not only as changes in urine.

lessons.title: Two tests that tell different stories
lessons.body: eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate) estimates how much blood your filters clean each minute. It is calculated from a blood test, creatinine, together with your age and sex. Think of it as how much water the plant can process. Urine albumin, usually reported as a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR), measures a protein that should mostly stay in the blood. Albumin leaking into urine means the filters are damaged, like a strainer whose holes are stretching. A person can have a normal eGFR but leaking albumin, or a low eGFR with little leak. International guidelines use both numbers together to judge risk, because together they predict what happens next far better than either alone.

lessons.title: Use results without guessing treatment
lessons.body: Keep a dated list of your results with the units printed on the report, because laboratories do not all use the same units. One result is a snapshot; the trend is the story. Creatinine can rise a little after a big meal of meat, heavy exercise, dehydration or certain medicines, so your team looks at the pattern and repeats tests before drawing conclusions. Ask: "How does this compare with last time? What would make you worried? Which change should make me call before my next visit?" Do not change medicines or diet on your own because of one number.

realSituation.title: Aling Cora's "normal" result
realSituation.body: Aling Cora, 52, has had diabetes for ten years. Her eGFR came back in the normal range, so she skipped her follow-up visit. Months later her doctor points to another line on the same report: urine albumin, clearly raised, and higher than the year before.
realSituation.debrief: Cora's filters were still processing enough blood, but they were leaking. That leak is an early warning that the filters are under strain from high sugar and high pressure, and it is exactly the stage when kidney-protecting treatment helps most. Her lesson: read both numbers, and ask about the trend, not only whether a result is flagged.

whatResearchShows.text: Chronic kidney disease is common. The Global Burden of Disease 2023 study estimated that 788 million adults worldwide had chronic kidney disease in 2023, about one in seven adults, and that it was the ninth leading cause of death. In the Philippines, health officials and kidney specialists have reported more than seven million affected people, most of them undiagnosed (press-reported figures). The KDIGO 2024 guideline recommends testing both eGFR and urine albumin, because the two together classify risk.

quiz.rationale: eGFR measures filtering amount; urine albumin shows filter damage. Leaking albumin is an early warning even when eGFR is normal.

Kidneys do not affect the rest of the body

quiz.rationale: Kidneys have a large reserve and fail quietly, so tests catch problems long before symptoms appear.

modules.title: Choose treatment through shared decisions
objectives: Name the main kidney care options
Identify the personal priorities you want your team to know
Ask for a balanced discussion of benefits, burdens and uncertainty
modules.everydayPicture: Choosing a kidney treatment is a little like choosing where to live. A doctor can tell you which houses are structurally safe and which are too far from the hospital. Only you know whether you need to be near your grandchildren, can manage stairs, or want a garden. A good decision needs both kinds of knowledge. When either side decides alone, the choice may be medically sound but unlivable, or livable but unsafe.

lessons.title: Options worth discussing
lessons.body: Depending on your condition, the options may include protecting the kidneys you have for as long as possible; hemodialysis, where a machine cleans your blood, usually in a unit about three times a week; peritoneal dialysis, where fluid placed in your belly cleans the blood using your own abdominal lining, usually at home; kidney transplantation from a living or deceased donor; and conservative kidney management, which is active care focused on comfort and quality of life without dialysis. Not every option suits every person, and local availability varies. Learning about an option never commits you to it.

lessons.title: What matters to you
lessons.body: Before the appointment, think about your life, not only your disease. How far is the nearest dialysis unit, and how will you get there? Do you work, and what are your hours? Who lives with you, and how much help do you want? Do you have a clean, dry space at home for supplies? What scares you most: needles, the cost, being a burden, losing your independence? Write your top three priorities. Ask the team: "For someone like me, what are the likely benefits, what are the burdens, and what do you not know?" Honest uncertainty is a sign of a good discussion, not a weak one.

lessons.title: A decision can be revisited
lessons.body: Ask what needs deciding now and what can wait. Many decisions in kidney care are steps, not final verdicts: you can start PD and move to hemodialysis, be listed for a transplant while on dialysis, or change your goals as life changes. Bring a supporter or ask for an interpreter if that helps you think clearly. Before you leave, ask when the plan will be reviewed and whom to call if your health, your preferences or your support at home change.

realSituation.title: Two neighbors, two right answers
realSituation.body: Two men in the same barangay reach kidney failure in the same month. Mang Tonio, 45, works as a security guard on rotating shifts and has a wife who is a nurse. Lolo Pedring, 84, has heart failure and memory problems and says his wish is to stay home with his apo.
realSituation.debrief: Tonio chooses PD so he can do exchanges around his shifts, with his wife trained as backup, and asks to be evaluated for a transplant. Pedring's family meets the kidney team, and together they choose conservative kidney management with close symptom care at home. Neither choice is wrong. The same medical facts led to different, well-informed plans because the priorities differed.

whatResearchShows.text: Decision aids, tools that lay out options with their benefits and harms, have strong evidence behind them. A 2024 Cochrane review of 209 randomized trials (more than 107,000 participants) found high-certainty evidence that decision aids improve knowledge and accuracy about risks, and moderate-certainty evidence that they help people make choices that match their values. The NICE (UK) kidney decision aid compares dialysis and conservative care side by side.

modules.title: Make medicines easier and safer
objectives: Keep one complete, current medicine list
Check any new medicine, herbal product or supplement before taking it
Know whom to ask when a dose is missed or you are sick
modules.everydayPicture: Most medicines leave the body through the liver, the kidneys or both. Picture a busy road with two exits. When the kidney exit narrows, cars that normally leave that way start to pile up. A dose that was perfect for healthy kidneys can build up to a harmful level when the kidneys are weak. That is why the same tablet can be safe for your neighbor and risky for you, and why the dose on the box is not always your dose.

lessons.title: One list to bring everywhere
lessons.body: Write every medicine you take: its name, what it is for, how much, and when. Include vitamins, herbal teas and capsules, creams, eye drops, injections such as insulin or erythropoietin, and anything bought without a prescription. Add your allergies and what happened. Bring the list, or a photo of it, to every appointment and every hospital visit, and update it the same day anything changes. After a hospital stay, lists often disagree; a pharmacist or your doctor can reconcile them so you follow one clear plan instead of two conflicting ones.

lessons.title: Ask before adding a product
lessons.body: Some everyday products are hard on kidneys. Pain relievers called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ibuprofen, mefenamic acid and naproxen) reduce blood flow into the kidney's filters and can cause sudden kidney injury, especially when you are dehydrated. Many herbal "kidney cleansers," detox teas and imported supplements are not tested for people with kidney disease; some contain potassium, heavy metals or hidden drugs. Before taking anything new, show the label to your pharmacist or kidney team and say: "I have kidney disease and I am on [your treatment]. Is this safe for me?"

lessons.title: Make a routine that survives real life
lessons.body: Link medicines to things you already do every day: breakfast, the morning news, brushing your teeth. A pill organizer or a phone alarm helps. Ask your team now, while you are well, what to do if you miss a dose, vomit, or have diarrhea or a fever, because some medicines should be paused on sick days and others must never be stopped. Write the answer down. Never double a dose to catch up or copy a friend's schedule. If cost, side effects or difficulty swallowing makes the plan hard, tell the team; there is often a cheaper or easier option.

realSituation.title: The pain reliever from the sari-sari store
realSituation.body: Tito Boy, 63, has CKD and high blood pressure. After helping move furniture for a fiesta, his back aches, so he buys mefenamic acid from the corner store and takes it three times a day for a week. It is hot, he drinks little water, and his legs begin to swell. His next blood test shows his kidney function has dropped.
realSituation.debrief: Two stresses hit at once: dehydration lowered blood flow to the kidneys, and the NSAID removed the kidneys' own protection against that drop. Stopping the drug and rehydrating under his doctor's care allowed partial recovery. A safer plan would have been one question to the pharmacist before buying. His medicine list now carries a line: "Avoid NSAIDs; ask first."

whatResearchShows.text: Medicine safety is one of the most practical skills in kidney care. The KDIGO 2024 guideline advises reviewing every medicine for kidney dosing and avoiding nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs where possible in people with CKD. Philippine kidney specialists have publicly warned about the uncritical use of food supplements (press-reported). Evidence linking herbal products to kidney injury comes mainly from case reports and observational studies, which is enough to justify asking first.

askYourTeam: Which of my medicines need a different dose because of my kidneys?
What should I do with each medicine if I am vomiting or have diarrhea?
Which pain reliever is safest for me?
modules.activity: Use W04 to practice a medicine list with fictional entries, one allergy and a refill reminder.
modules.teachBack: Show how you would ask a pharmacist about a new supplement, including what you would tell them about your kidneys.

quiz.stem: You miss a dose and do not have instructions. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Check with your pharmacist or prescribing team
Automatically double the next dose
Copy a friend's dialysis-day routine

quiz.rationale: The correct response depends on the medicine and your individual plan.

quiz.stem: A relative brings a herbal "kidney cleanser" from abroad. What is the best response?

options.text: Take it because it is natural
Show the label to your pharmacist or kidney team before taking it
Take half the dose to be safe

quiz.rationale: Natural does not mean safe for weak kidneys. Some products contain potassium, metals or hidden drugs.

quiz.stem: Why can a normal dose of some medicines become harmful in kidney disease?

options.text: Weak kidneys clear some medicines more slowly, so they can build up
Kidney disease makes all medicines stronger in the stomach
It cannot; doses never change

quiz.rationale: When the kidney exit narrows, drugs that leave through it accumulate, so doses may need adjusting.

modules.title: Build a food plan that fits your life
objectives: Explain why kidney diets are individual
Read the sodium line on a food label and count servings
Plan affordable Filipino meals with your dietitian
modules.everydayPicture: Food advice for kidney disease is often handed out like a list of enemies: no banana, no tomato, no dried fish, no soy sauce. The list feels simple, but it breaks down quickly. A person early in CKD may need to cut salt but eat plenty of vegetables, while a person on dialysis may need more protein, not less. A list written for someone else can leave you hungry, weak and no safer. The better picture is a tailor-made barong: measured for you, and adjusted when your body changes.

lessons.title: Start with your own plan
lessons.body: Your food plan depends on your stage of kidney disease, your treatment, your blood results, your appetite, your weight and other conditions such as diabetes. Salt is the one change that helps almost everyone: sodium makes the body hold water, which raises blood pressure and strains both the heart and the kidneys. Potassium, phosphorus, protein and fluid limits depend on your results and treatment. Ask your dietitian which one or two changes matter most right now, rather than trying to change everything at once.

lessons.title: Use the meals you already eat
lessons.body: Bring real examples to your dietitian: sinigang, tinola, adobo, pancit, rice with fried fish, champorado. Most can be adapted. Season with calamansi, garlic, onion, ginger, pepper and herbs instead of extra patis, toyo, bagoong and seasoning cubes. On packaged foods, find sodium per serving on the nutrition label, then count how many servings you actually eat; one pack of instant noodles is often two servings. Ask how cooking methods, such as boiling vegetables and discarding the water, change what is in the food, and what affordable substitutes are available at your market.

lessons.title: Avoid making the plan too restrictive
lessons.body: Cutting whole food groups because another patient was told to can cause poor nutrition, muscle loss and constipation, and muscle loss itself worsens outcomes in kidney disease. Report poor appetite, unplanned weight loss, or a diet so strict you have stopped enjoying meals. A dietitian can loosen what is safe to loosen. Your plan should change when your treatment changes: what was right before dialysis is often wrong after it.

realSituation.title: Aling Nena gives up vegetables
realSituation.body: Aling Nena, 67, read in a group chat that "kidney patients must avoid vegetables and fruit." For three months she eats rice, eggs and canned meat loaf. She feels weak, is constipated, and her blood pressure is higher, not lower.
realSituation.debrief: The canned meat was loaded with sodium, and removing vegetables took away fiber and nutrients she did not need to give up. Her own laboratory results showed normal potassium. Her dietitian restores most vegetables, swaps the canned meat for fresh fish and chicken, and teaches her to read labels. Within weeks she feels stronger. The group chat's rule was written for a different person.

whatResearchShows.text: The KDOQI (Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative) 2020 nutrition guideline, developed with the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, recommends individualized medical nutrition therapy by a dietitian rather than one standard diet. The World Health Organization advises adults generally to keep sodium under 2 grams a day (about one teaspoon of salt); the average Filipino intake has been estimated at about double that (WHO estimate, press-reported). Your own team may set a different target.

askYourTeam: Which one or two food changes matter most for me right now?
Do I need to limit potassium, phosphorus, protein or fluid, based on my own results?
Can you help me adapt the dishes my family cooks?
modules.activity: On W05, redesign one familiar meal using your own dietitian's priorities; circle any question you still need answered.
modules.teachBack: Explain why a dialysis meal plan may differ from an earlier CKD plan.

quiz.stem: A friend says all kidney patients must avoid the same foods. What should you do?

options.text: Adopt every restriction immediately
Stop eating vegetables entirely
Use advice based on your own treatment and results

quiz.rationale: Nutrition needs are individualized; excessive restriction can create new problems.

quiz.stem: A nutrition label lists the sodium for one serving, and the pack contains two servings. You eat the whole pack. How much sodium did you eat?

options.text: The amount on the label
Twice the amount on the label
Half the amount on the label

quiz.rationale: Label values are per serving. Multiply by the number of servings you actually eat.

quiz.stem: Why does cutting salt help most people with kidney disease?

options.text: Sodium makes the body hold water, raising blood pressure and straining the heart and kidneys
Salt directly destroys kidney filters on contact
It does not help anyone

quiz.rationale: Sodium pulls water with it. Less sodium means less fluid retention and lower blood pressure.

modules.title: Follow your own fluid and monitoring plan
objectives: Find your personal fluid plan, if you have one
Record home measurements with date, time and units
Know which symptoms need action even when numbers look fine
modules.everydayPicture: Healthy kidneys work like a smart overflow drain: drink more and they release more, drink less and they hold on. As kidney function falls, especially on dialysis when urine output drops, the drain slows or closes. Water you drink stays in the body until the next treatment removes it. Extra fluid first collects in the legs and around the eyes, then in the lungs, where it makes breathing hard. That is why some people need a fluid limit and others do not, and why the limit is personal.

lessons.title: Your targets belong to your care plan
lessons.body: Ask your team whether you need a fluid limit at all. If you do, ask how much, and how they want you to count it: soup, sabaw, ice, coffee, juice and fruits like watermelon all contain water. Your limit depends largely on how much urine you still make and on your treatment, so it can change over time. This course will never give you a daily amount. A number borrowed from another patient may be too strict for you, causing dehydration, or too loose, causing fluid overload.

lessons.title: A useful record
lessons.body: If your team asks for home weights or blood pressure readings, learn to use the equipment with them. Weigh yourself at the same time each day, on the same scale, wearing similar clothes. Write the date, time, number and unit (kilograms, mmHg) and any symptom. Ask what range your team expects and what to do when a reading is outside it. Sudden weight gain over a day or two is usually water, not fat, and it is an early signal worth reporting.

lessons.title: Symptoms still matter
lessons.body: A reassuring number does not cancel a serious symptom. If you have new severe breathlessness, cannot lie flat, have chest pain, faint, or become confused, seek emergency help immediately, whatever the scale says. For smaller changes, such as more swelling or a steady rise in weight, use the contact plan agreed with your team. Recording a measurement is your job; changing treatment because of it is the team's decision.

realSituation.title: Kuya Jun's birthday weekend
realSituation.body: Kuya Jun, 41, has been on hemodialysis for two years and passes very little urine. Over a long weekend he attends two parties with plenty of soup, soft drinks and ice. On Monday morning his ankles are swollen, and he feels short of breath when he lies down.
realSituation.debrief: With almost no urine, every glass stayed in Jun's body for three days instead of the usual two. Breathlessness lying flat suggests fluid reaching the lungs. He calls his unit, which brings his session forward and reviews his fluid plan with him. Next fiesta, he plans ahead: smaller cups, ice chips counted as fluid, and less salty food so he is less thirsty.

whatResearchShows.text: In the international Dialysis Outcomes and Practice Patterns Study (DOPPS), very large weight gains between sessions were associated with about 12% higher mortality. This is an observational association, and sicker patients may gain more weight, but it supports careful, individual fluid planning. Salt reduction lowers thirst, which makes any fluid plan easier to follow.

askYourTeam: Do I need a fluid limit, and if so, how should I count it?
What weight or blood pressure range do you expect for me at home?
At what point should I call you about weight gain or swelling?
modules.activity: On W06, enter a fictional weight and blood pressure reading with units, and write who provides your actual thresholds.
modules.teachBack: Explain the difference between recording a measurement and changing treatment.

quiz.stem: Where should your personal daily fluid amount come from?

options.text: The amount another patient drinks
Your treating team's current plan
A universal amount supplied by this course

quiz.rationale: A generic course cannot prescribe an individual fluid allowance. It depends on your urine output and treatment.

quiz.stem: Your weight is within your usual range, but you suddenly cannot breathe lying down. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it because the weight is fine
Seek urgent help; a serious symptom matters more than a reassuring number
Drink more water

quiz.rationale: Severe breathlessness needs urgent assessment no matter what the scale says.

quiz.stem: Why do some people on dialysis need a fluid limit when others do not?

options.text: Because people who make little urine keep most of what they drink until the next treatment
Because water damages dialysis machines
Because everyone on dialysis has the same limit

quiz.rationale: Remaining urine output largely decides how much fluid the body can clear between treatments.

modules.title: Prevent infection and protect your access
objectives: Clean your hands the way your setting teaches
Recognize early signs of an access or exit-site infection
Ask for a vaccination review
modules.everydayPicture: Your skin is a wall that keeps germs out. Every dialysis access is a planned doorway through that wall: a fistula or graft is a door opened with needles and closed after each session, while a catheter or PD tube is a door that stays slightly open all the time. Doors that stay open let in more uninvited guests. Kidney disease also weakens the body's guards, the immune system, so an infection that starts small can travel into the blood quickly. Clean hands and a well-kept doorway are your strongest protection.

lessons.title: Hands and shared spaces
lessons.body: Most germs that reach an access travel on hands. Clean your hands with soap and water or an alcohol hand rub before touching your access, dressing or supplies, after using the toilet, and after handling pets or garbage. Ask your educator to show you the exact method your unit uses and watch you do it once. Tell staff before your session if you have a fever, cough, diarrhea or a skin wound, so they can protect you and other patients. Wearing a mask when you have a cough protects the people sitting next to you in the unit.

lessons.title: Know your doorway
lessons.body: Ask which access you have and how to care for it daily. A fistula joins an artery directly to a vein in your arm; a graft uses a soft tube to connect them; a hemodialysis catheter is a tube placed in a large neck or chest vein; a PD catheter enters the belly. Keep catheter dressings clean and dry as taught, and never open a catheter cap, flush it, or remove a dressing to look at a problem yourself; that is how germs get a direct route into the bloodstream. Wash a fistula or graft arm with soap and water before every session.

lessons.title: Report rather than hide changes
lessons.body: Report redness, warmth, swelling, pain, pus or any drainage at an access or exit site, and any fever or shaking chills, especially during or after dialysis. Shaking chills during a session can mean germs entering the blood. Do not wait for the next routine visit because you feel embarrassed or do not want to trouble anyone. Ask your team which vaccines suit you, such as hepatitis B, influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, because people with kidney disease respond less strongly to infections and to some vaccines.

realSituation.title: Ate Grace's damp dressing
realSituation.body: Ate Grace, 36, has a tunneled catheter while her fistula matures. During the rainy season she bathes with a dipper and the dressing gets wet. She notices a little redness at the exit site but decides to wait for Thursday's session. On Wednesday night she has shaking chills.
realSituation.debrief: A wet dressing lets skin germs travel along the outside of the catheter; chills suggest they reached her blood. She goes to the emergency department, receives blood cultures and antibiotics, and recovers. Her unit teaches her a covered bathing method and asks her to call the same day for redness. Her fistula is now checked at every visit so the catheter can come out sooner.

whatResearchShows.text: Access type strongly affects infection risk. A CDC Vital Signs report found that adults on hemodialysis had about 100 times the rate of Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection of adults not on dialysis, and that central venous catheters carried about six times the risk of fistulas in national surveillance data (2017 to 2020, United States). The KDOQI 2019 vascular access guideline asks teams to plan each person's access as part of a lifelong "ESKD Life-Plan."

askYourTeam: What kind of access do I have, and how should I care for it every day?
Which signs at my access or exit site mean I should call the same day?
Which vaccines do you recommend for me?

modules.teachBack: Explain whom you would contact about new access drainage, and why you would not wait for your next visit.

quiz.stem: Your catheter dressing is wet and loose. What is the best action?

options.text: Contact the dialysis team promptly for instructions and dressing care
Remove it and manipulate the catheter yourself
Wait until the next routine appointment without calling

quiz.rationale: A compromised dressing requires trained assessment and care.

quiz.stem: You get shaking chills during a dialysis session. What should you do?

options.text: Stay quiet until the session ends
Tell the nurse immediately
Pull the blankets up and sleep

quiz.rationale: Chills during dialysis can signal a bloodstream infection and need immediate assessment.

quiz.stem: Which access type carries the highest infection risk?

options.text: Fistula
Graft
Hemodialysis catheter

quiz.rationale: A catheter is a doorway that stays open, which is why teams work to replace catheters with a fistula or graft when possible.

modules.title: Recognize urgent problems and get help
objectives: Identify symptoms that need emergency help now
Give a clear, 30-second help request
Keep emergency information where you and your family can find it
modules.everydayPicture: Most kidney problems unfold over weeks. A few unfold over minutes. Potassium that climbs too high can disturb the heart's rhythm with little warning; fluid can flood the lungs overnight; a fistula carries blood under high pressure, so a bleed can be heavy. These are the moments when the right action is not to search online, message a group chat or wait for clinic hours, but to get emergency help. Knowing the list ahead of time turns panic into a plan.

lessons.title: Act on severe symptoms
lessons.body: Get emergency help immediately for: severe or worsening breathlessness, or being unable to lie flat; chest pain or pressure; fainting or collapse; new confusion, severe drowsiness, or difficulty speaking; new weakness of the face, arm or leg; heavy or spurting bleeding from an access; and a seizure. Severe muscle weakness or a very slow or irregular heartbeat in someone who has missed dialysis can be a sign of dangerous potassium. In the dialysis unit, call staff at once. Outside the unit, use your local emergency service or go to the nearest emergency department.

lessons.title: Say the important details
lessons.body: Responders work faster with clear facts. Practice saying: where you are (with a landmark), what is happening, when it started, that the person has kidney disease and which treatment (hemodialysis, PD or transplant), and whether there is active bleeding. If you can, bring the medicine and allergy list and the dialysis or transplant contact card. Tell emergency staff the arm with a fistula or graft should not be used for blood pressure or drips. Do not delay urgent care to finish a form or wait for a reply to a message.

lessons.title: Prepare before an emergency
lessons.body: Ask your team for written instructions for the emergencies that fit your treatment, such as how to apply pressure to a bleeding access, and have them show you. Keep the contact card on the refrigerator and a photo on every family phone. Rehearse once with your household: who calls, who brings the list, who stays with the patient. Remember that this website, a chatbot, a quiz or an online message is not a monitored emergency service; no one is watching it in real time.

realSituation.title: The 30-second call
realSituation.body: At 2 a.m., Lola Fe, 74, on hemodialysis, wakes gasping and cannot lie down. Her grandson Paolo, 19, panics and starts typing her symptoms into a search engine.
realSituation.debrief: Paolo remembers the family rehearsal and calls for emergency help instead: "I'm at Purok 3, near the chapel, in Santa Rita. My grandmother is on dialysis, she can't breathe lying down, it started an hour ago. No bleeding." He sits her upright, grabs the medicine list and the unit card from the refrigerator, and goes with her. At the emergency department the team finds fluid in her lungs and arranges urgent dialysis. The rehearsal saved minutes that mattered.

whatResearchShows.text: Missing or delaying dialysis increases the risk of fluid overload and high potassium, both of which can be life-threatening. In DOPPS, skipping one or more sessions a month was associated with about 30% higher mortality (observational data). Rehearsed emergency plans are standard practice in kidney units; their value rests on common sense and clinical experience more than on trials.

askYourTeam: What are the emergency signs that matter most for my treatment?
Can you show me how to stop bleeding from my access?
Which emergency department or unit should we go to after hours?

modules.teachBack: Name two situations in which you would seek emergency help without waiting for a clinic callback.

quiz.stem: Someone has heavy access bleeding and feels faint. What is the priority?

options.text: Wait for a routine appointment
Finish an online symptom questionnaire first
Activate emergency help immediately and follow the taught bleeding first-aid plan

quiz.rationale: Heavy bleeding with faintness can be life-threatening; online assessment must not delay care.

quiz.stem: A person on dialysis has new chest pain at home. What should the family do?

options.text: Post in the patients' group chat and wait for advice
Get emergency help now
Wait until the next dialysis session

quiz.rationale: Chest pain needs emergency assessment immediately. No website or chat is monitored as an emergency service.

quiz.stem: Which detail is most useful to tell emergency responders?

options.text: Your favorite food
Your location, what is happening, and your kidney treatment
The name of your barangay captain

quiz.rationale: Location, the problem, and the kidney treatment help responders act quickly and safely.

modules.title: Manage tiredness, emotions and daily activity
objectives: Describe how symptoms affect your day, without blame
Set a realistic activity goal with your team
Ask early for emotional or practical support
modules.everydayPicture: Kidney disease is often described by numbers, but people live it through symptoms: tiredness that does not lift after sleep, itching at night, cramps, poor appetite, low mood. Many people assume these are just the price of being sick and never mention them. That assumption breaks down because many symptoms have causes that can be found and treated: anemia, poor sleep, high phosphorus, depression, under-dialysis or medicine side effects. You cannot get help for a symptom no one knows about.

lessons.title: Describe the effect on your day
lessons.body: Use plain words and concrete examples. Instead of "I'm tired," try "I can no longer climb the stairs to my apartment without stopping twice" or "After dialysis I sleep until evening and miss my grandchildren's visit." Say when the symptom happens, how long it lasts and what it stops you doing. Ask which symptoms need tests. Tiredness can come from anemia, the low red blood cell count that is common in kidney disease, and that is treatable.

lessons.title: Move, pace and reconnect
lessons.body: Regular physical activity is one of the best-proven ways to feel stronger with kidney disease. Walking, gentle strength exercises with light weights or water bottles, and stretching all count. Start small, such as a ten-minute walk around the plaza, and build up gradually with your team's approval. Some units offer pedaling during dialysis. Plan rest around treatment days. Worries about work, intimacy, body image or faith are part of health too; you may raise them privately with a doctor, nurse or social worker.

lessons.title: Support is part of care
lessons.body: About one in four people with kidney disease experiences depression, which is more than ordinary sadness: it can sap motivation, sleep and appetite, and it is treatable. Tell someone you trust if coping becomes hard, and ask for a counselor, social worker or mental health referral. Patient groups and faith communities can help you feel less alone. If you ever feel unable to keep yourself safe or think about harming yourself, seek emergency help immediately and stay with a trusted person.

realSituation.title: Manong Ben stops going out
realSituation.body: Manong Ben, 66, a retired teacher on hemodialysis, used to lead the parish choir. Over six months he stops attending, sleeps most afternoons, and tells his wife there is no point. He has never mentioned any of this at the unit because "everyone there is tired."
realSituation.debrief: His wife encourages him to tell the nurse. His team finds low hemoglobin, adjusts his anemia treatment, screens him for depression and refers him to a counselor. A physical therapist starts him on short walks. Three months later he is back in the choir for one Mass a week. Not every symptom can be fixed, but several of Ben's could, and none would have been found if he had kept quiet.

whatResearchShows.text: A meta-analysis of 249 study populations (55,982 participants) found interview-diagnosed depression in about 23% of people on dialysis, and about one in four adults with CKD overall. A Cochrane review of 45 randomized trials (1,863 participants) found that regular exercise improved fitness, walking capacity, blood pressure and health-related quality of life in adults with CKD, although many trials were small and at risk of bias.

askYourTeam: Could my tiredness have a treatable cause, such as anemia?
What kind of exercise is safe for me, and how should I start?
Can I talk with a counselor or social worker?

options.text: Hide it to avoid troubling the clinic
Describe it to the care team and ask for assessment
Assume no one can help

quiz.rationale: Symptoms and distress deserve clinical attention; several causes of tiredness are treatable.

quiz.stem: What is the best way to start exercising with kidney disease?

Start small, build up gradually, and agree the plan with your team
Avoid all movement to save energy

quiz.rationale: Gradual, team-approved activity is safe and improves fitness and quality of life.

options.text: Wait for the next routine visit
Seek emergency help immediately and stay with them
Tell them to sleep it off

quiz.rationale: Thoughts of self-harm are an emergency. Get immediate help and do not leave the person alone.

modules.title: Understand Philippine benefits and treatment costs
objectives: Tell the difference between a benefit paid to a facility and cash paid to you
Ask for a current eligibility check and itemized explanation
Recognize that each treatment has its own policy and effective date
modules.everydayPicture: A PhilHealth benefit works more like a bill-paying arrangement than a cash allowance. PhilHealth pays the accredited facility for covered services delivered to an eligible member, according to the rules in a specific circular. The picture breaks down when people hear a package amount on the news and assume it is money they will receive, or that every expense is covered. Knowing which policy applies, and asking for it in writing, protects your budget.

lessons.title: Know the benefit category
lessons.body: Under PhilHealth Circular 2024-0023, eligible members with stage 5 chronic kidney disease who are registered in the PhilHealth Dialysis Database can receive coverage for up to 156 hemodialysis sessions per calendar year, at a package rate of PHP 6,350 per session, paid to the accredited facility. That is roughly three sessions a week for a year. These are payments to the provider for covered treatment, not cash given to you. Ask the facility to confirm your registration, eligibility and how many sessions remain.

lessons.title: Ask before signing
lessons.body: Ask the benefits officer to explain, in a language you understand, which services the package covers, whether any charges are optional, and what you would pay. Ask for an itemized bill. Keep copies of every document you sign and every receipt. If something is unclear, ask how to raise a concern or file a complaint. Other help may be available, such as government medical assistance programs, local government units, charity offices and patient groups; a social worker can help you find them.

lessons.title: Check the right policy
lessons.body: Peritoneal dialysis, kidney transplant surgery and care after transplant are covered by separate circulars with their own rules, and policies are revised. A circular can be published on one date and take effect later. Ask: "Which policy applies to me, and from what date?" Bring benefit questions to the facility coordinator or PhilHealth directly rather than relying on a social media post or an advertised maximum.

realSituation.title: The rate in the news
realSituation.body: Mang Celso, 55, hears on the radio that PhilHealth "gives P6,350 per dialysis." He expects nothing to pay and is upset when the unit asks him to sign a form and mentions a charge for a medicine given during dialysis.
realSituation.debrief: The benefits officer explains that the package is paid to the unit for covered services, shows him the itemized list, and explains which medicine is outside the package and why. She checks his registration and remaining sessions and refers him to the hospital's medical social service for help with the extra cost. Celso leaves with copies of everything and a clear number, not a rumor.

whatResearchShows.text: These are policy facts, not research findings, and they change. The hemodialysis package figures above come from PhilHealth Circular 2024-0023 and PhilHealth's public benefit listing, checked November 28, 2026. Peritoneal dialysis and transplant figures are deliberately not quoted here until their full circulars and annexes are verified. Always confirm the current rules with your facility.

askYourTeam: Am I registered in the PhilHealth Dialysis Database, and how many sessions do I have left this year?
What does the package cover, and what might I pay?
Which other assistance programs can help with my costs?

A guarantee that every unrelated expense is covered

modules.title: Plan for travel, typhoons and interrupted care
objectives: Prepare a portable treatment folder
Arrange a backup unit and backup contact
Avoid unsafe do-it-yourself substitutes when care is interrupted
modules.everydayPicture: For most people, a flooded road means a missed day of work. For someone on dialysis, it can mean missing the treatment that removes potassium and fluid. Because kidney failure does not pause for weather, planning must happen while roads are open. Think of the plan as a spare tire: you hope never to use it, but finding it in the dark on a flooded road is the worst time to start looking.

lessons.title: Plan while services are open
lessons.body: Ask your unit now: How will you announce schedule changes during a typhoon signal, flood, earthquake or power outage? Is there a backup unit we can go to? Whom do we call if your number does not answer? For travel to the province or abroad, arrange dialysis at the receiving unit weeks ahead; they will usually need your recent laboratory results, hepatitis tests and treatment prescription. PD and transplant patients should plan supply deliveries and medicine refills before the storm season.

lessons.title: Prepare a portable folder
lessons.body: Keep a waterproof folder or sealed plastic bag with: your treatment summary and prescription, medicine and allergy list, latest laboratory results, PhilHealth details, the contact card for your unit and a backup unit, and a few days of medicines. Keep a phone power bank charged. PD patients should store supplies off the floor, away from floodwater, and ask what emergency stock is right for them. Ask your team whether you need any written emergency diet instructions for days when dialysis is delayed.

lessons.title: If a session or exchange is disrupted
lessons.body: Contact your unit or backup service as soon as you know you cannot attend, even if it is a short delay. Follow your written contingency plan. Do not ration prescribed medicines, change dialysis settings, or invent a replacement schedule. If dialysis is delayed, your team may advise limiting salty foods, fluid and potassium-rich foods until your next session, according to your own plan. Seek emergency help if severe symptoms appear.

realSituation.title: Signal No. 3 in Bicol
realSituation.body: Aling Rosa, 59, dialyzes Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays in Legazpi. A typhoon is forecast to make landfall on a Wednesday. On Monday, the unit announces it will add Tuesday sessions for patients whose routes may flood.
realSituation.debrief: Because Rosa kept the unit's number and joined their announcement group, she moves her session to Tuesday. She packs her waterproof folder, charges her power bank and arranges a ride with her nephew. When roads stay closed until Friday afternoon, she calls the backup unit on her card, limits salty food and fluids as her written plan instructs, and dialyzes there on Friday evening. She missed no treatment.

whatResearchShows.text: The Philippines is one of the most typhoon-exposed countries in the world, and disruptions to dialysis after disasters are well documented internationally. Experience from disaster response shows that patients with a written plan, a backup unit and early contact with their service are less likely to miss treatment. Evidence here comes from disaster reports and expert consensus rather than trials.

modules.title: Speak up, protect privacy and review your plan
objectives: Use teach-back to check that you understood
Choose what your care partner may know
Prepare a short agenda for your next care review
modules.everydayPicture: Many people nod in the clinic and only realize at home that they did not understand. It is not a lack of intelligence; health information is new language delivered quickly, often to someone who is tired or worried. Speaking up is not disrespect. In good kidney care, the team wants you to ask, because a question in the clinic is far cheaper than a mistake at home.

lessons.title: Ask until the plan is clear
lessons.body: Try these phrases: "Please show me." "Can you write that down?" "Let me explain it back so you can check I understood." If you use a language other than the one being spoken, ask for an interpreter or bring someone you trust. You can raise concerns about your care respectfully, and you can ask for a second opinion. A good team will not be offended.

lessons.title: Your information and your supporter
lessons.body: Your health information belongs to you. In the Philippines, the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act 10173) treats health information as sensitive personal information that needs special protection. Decide who may join your consultations and what they may be told. A relative being present does not automatically give them permission to see all your records. Ask the facility how it handles consent, how to request your records, and how to file a complaint.

lessons.title: Make the next appointment useful
lessons.body: Before each review, write your top three questions, bring your medicine list and any home records, and note what has changed: new symptoms, hospital visits, money or transport problems. At the end, ask: "What has changed in my plan? Who does the next step? When do we meet again?" Revisit your learning path whenever your treatment, your health or your care partner changes.

realSituation.title: Nodding in the clinic
realSituation.body: Ate Mylene, 48, a market vendor, is told her medicines will change. She nods, but at home she cannot remember which tablet to stop. Her cousin, who came along, tells the rest of the family about her diagnosis without asking her.
realSituation.debrief: At the next visit, Mylene uses teach-back: "So I stop the white tablet in the morning and start the new one at night?" The nurse corrects one detail and writes it down. Mylene also tells the team that only her husband may receive updates, and she asks her cousin to keep her health private. One sentence of teach-back and one clear sharing preference prevented two different problems.

whatResearchShows.text: Teach-back improved knowledge, self-management and self-confidence in a systematic review of kidney patient education, although trials were small and varied. Privacy protections for health information are set out in Republic Act 10173 and its implementing rules.

modules.title: Protect kidney health before dialysis
objectives: Name your personal kidney-protection priorities
Plan regular monitoring even when you feel well
Prepare a sick-day question for your team
modules.everydayPicture: Picture the kidney filters as clay pots under a dripping roof. High blood pressure is water hitting the pots too hard; high blood sugar is water that is sticky and corrosive; smoking narrows the pipes that feed them. Each drip does a little damage, and lost filters do not grow back. But fix the roof early and the remaining pots can last for decades. Kidney protection is less about one big treatment and more about stopping many small drips.

lessons.title: Choose priorities with your clinician
lessons.body: Ask how blood pressure, blood sugar (if you have diabetes), weight, smoking and your medicines affect your kidneys. Your clinician sets your targets and treatment based on your situation; they are not the same for everyone. High pressure inside the filters, called glomerular hypertension, is one of the main forces that wears them out, which is why several kidney-protecting medicines work by lowering it. Feeling well does not mean the damage has stopped; kidney disease is usually silent.

lessons.title: Build a repeatable routine
lessons.body: Link medicines to daily habits and write your appointments on a calendar the family can see. Ask how often to repeat blood and urine tests, which is usually decided by your eGFR, urine albumin and how fast they are changing. Stop smoking, and ask for help doing so. Move most days. If cost, work hours or travel make follow-up hard, tell the team early; there are often cheaper medicines, closer laboratories or PhilHealth Konsulta services that can help.

lessons.title: Prepare for illness
lessons.body: Vomiting, diarrhea, fever and not eating can dry you out and cause a sudden drop in kidney function, called acute kidney injury (AKI). Some medicines, including certain blood pressure and diabetes medicines, may need to be paused during such illness and restarted afterward, but the right list is individual. Ask your clinician for written sick-day instructions that name your own medicines, and whom to call. Do not stop or restart a medicine based on a generic online list.

realSituation.title: Sir Arnel's stomach flu
realSituation.body: Sir Arnel, 50, a public school teacher with CKD and diabetes, catches stomach flu during exam week. He keeps taking all his medicines while barely eating or drinking for two days and feels dizzy when standing.
realSituation.debrief: Dehydration plus medicines that lower blood pressure and filter pressure caused his kidney function to dip. Because he had asked for a sick-day plan at his last visit, he finds the written card, sees which two medicines to pause, calls the clinic, and gets a blood test. His function recovers within a week, and he restarts the medicines as instructed. The card turned an emergency into a phone call.

whatResearchShows.text: People who survive an episode of acute kidney injury in hospital have a higher long-term risk of death, dialysis and chronic kidney disease than matched people without AKI (meta-analysis of 14 studies, over a million patients, 2026). The KDIGO 2024 guideline recommends regular eGFR and urine albumin monitoring, blood pressure and glucose control, lifestyle measures, and medication review for people with CKD.

modules.title: Prepare for changing kidney care needs
objectives: Start conversations about future treatment early
Identify practical barriers and supports
Leave each visit with a written next step
modules.everydayPicture: Starting dialysis in an emergency is like moving house during a flood: everything is rushed, and the choices are made for you. People who plan ahead are more likely to start with a ready access, a chosen treatment and a family that knows what to expect. Planning is not giving up hope. It is packing the bag early so that, if the day comes, you walk out the door instead of being carried.

lessons.title: Preparation is a conversation
lessons.body: Ask your kidney team when to begin talking about future treatment. Many teams start this education when kidney function is falling steadily or is around a quarter of normal, but timing depends on your condition, how fast it is changing and your wishes. Planning may include visiting a dialysis unit, meeting a PD nurse, being referred for transplant evaluation, or meeting a supportive care team. An access, such as a fistula, often needs months to mature, which is one reason early planning matters.

lessons.title: Bring real-life information
lessons.body: Tell the team about your travel distance, income, work, housing, hand strength, eyesight, who can help you and what you hope for. These details change which options are realistic. Ask which services are available locally, how each would fit your week, and what PhilHealth and other programs would cover. A social worker can help with benefits and transport.

lessons.title: Leave with a next step
lessons.body: At the end of each visit, write down who will arrange the next referral, what the next appointment is, and how to ask questions while waiting. Learning about dialysis or transplant does not mean you must start now, and many people with slowly changing kidney function never need dialysis. Preparation keeps the choice in your hands.

realSituation.title: Two ways to start dialysis
realSituation.body: Nanay Lourdes and Tatay Rodel both reach kidney failure in the same year. Lourdes had met a PD nurse and had a fistula created six months earlier. Rodel had skipped visits because he felt fine, and arrives at the emergency department breathless.
realSituation.debrief: Lourdes starts dialysis on a planned date using her matured fistula and goes home the same day. Rodel needs an urgent catheter in his neck and a week in hospital, and his family must choose a unit in a hurry. Both now do well, but Rodel's start was harder, riskier and more expensive. The difference was not luck; it was preparation.

whatResearchShows.text: Starting hemodialysis with a catheter rather than a fistula or graft is associated with more infections and hospital stays, which is why the KDOQI 2019 guideline asks teams to plan access early as part of each person's ESKD Life-Plan. Structured pre-dialysis education and decision aids help people make informed choices (Cochrane 2024).

modules.title: The heart, kidney and sugar connection, and kidney-protecting medicines
objectives: Explain why kidney, heart and blood sugar problems travel together
Name the families of medicines that protect kidneys, as questions to ask
Understand why a small early dip in eGFR can be expected with some medicines
modules.everydayPicture: The heart, the kidneys and the body's sugar and fat handling are linked like three gears in one clock. When one gear slips, the others strain: diabetes damages kidney filters, failing kidneys raise blood pressure and stiffen arteries, and a weak heart starves the kidneys of blood flow. Doctors now call this the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) connection. The good news is that some medicines turn all three gears in the right direction at once.

lessons.title: Why these conditions travel together
lessons.body: Diabetes and high blood pressure are the two leading causes of kidney failure in the Philippines. High sugar damages the small blood vessels in the filters; high pressure batters them. As kidney function falls, the body holds salt and water, blood pressure rises, and calcium can deposit in arteries. That is why many people with CKD are more likely to have a heart attack or stroke than to need dialysis, and why your kidney team cares about your cholesterol, weight and heart as well as your kidneys.

lessons.title: Medicines that protect, as questions to ask
lessons.body: Several medicine families have strong evidence for slowing kidney damage. Blood pressure medicines called ACE inhibitors and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) relax the outflow vessel of each filter, lowering the pressure inside it. SGLT2 inhibitors, first made for diabetes, help the kidney sense that it is getting enough salt, which reduces filter pressure and protects the heart too. Others include a newer non-steroidal medicine called finerenone and, for some people with diabetes, GLP-1 receptor agonists. Not everyone can take them. This lesson does not recommend any medicine for you; it gives you the right question: "Is one of these right for me?"

lessons.title: A small early dip can be expected
lessons.body: Because these medicines lower the pressure inside the filters, eGFR often dips slightly in the first weeks, like easing off the accelerator to save the engine. Your team will check blood tests after starting and decide whether the dip is the expected kind. Do not stop the medicine yourself because of one result. Also ask about sick-day pauses, low blood pressure symptoms and, for SGLT2 inhibitors, keeping the genital area clean, since sugar in the urine can encourage yeast infections.

realSituation.title: Ma'am Lyn's worrying dip
realSituation.body: Ma'am Lyn, 57, an accountant with diabetes and CKD, starts an SGLT2 inhibitor. Four weeks later her eGFR is a little lower. A friend says the medicine is "killing her kidneys," and she considers stopping it.
realSituation.debrief: Lyn calls her nephrologist instead. He explains the expected early dip from lower filter pressure, checks that it is small, and repeats the test. Over the next year her eGFR declines more slowly than before, and her urine albumin falls. The early dip was the sign the medicine was working the way it should.

whatResearchShows.text: In the DAPA-CKD trial (4,304 people with CKD, with or without diabetes), dapagliflozin reduced the combined risk of major kidney decline, kidney failure or death from kidney or heart causes from 14.5% to 9.2% over about 2.4 years: one event prevented for every 19 people treated. In EMPA-KIDNEY (6,609 people), empagliflozin reduced kidney progression or cardiovascular death from 16.9% to 13.1% over two years. KDIGO 2024 strongly recommends SGLT2 inhibitors for many adults with CKD. Suitability is decided individually.

modules.title: Navigate a hemodialysis treatment day
objectives: Prepare for each session
Report symptoms during treatment early
Plan a safe trip home
modules.everydayPicture: During hemodialysis, your blood travels out through a needle or catheter, through a filter called a dialyzer, and back again. The dialyzer is a bundle of thousands of hair-thin hollow fibers. Blood flows inside the fibers, cleaning fluid called dialysate flows around them in the opposite direction, and waste and extra minerals cross the fiber walls from the side with more to the side with less. At the same time the machine gently pulls off extra water. Removing two or three days' worth of fluid in about four hours is why some people feel cramps or dizziness, and why reporting early helps.

lessons.title: Before the session
lessons.body: Arrive on time and tell the nurse about anything new since your last session: illness, a hospital or clinic visit, new medicines, bleeding, a fall, or changes at your access. Staff will check your identity, weigh you and take your blood pressure; the weight helps them decide how much fluid to remove. Wash your access arm if you have a fistula or graft. Ask your team which medicines to take before dialysis and which to take after, because some blood pressure medicines can make you dizzy during treatment.

lessons.title: During treatment
lessons.body: Tell staff promptly about cramps, dizziness, nausea, headache, chest pain, itching, breathlessness or any pain at the access. Early reports let the team adjust fluid removal or treatment before a symptom becomes a fall in blood pressure. Keep your access visible so staff can see that needles and lines are secure. Machine alarms are normal parts of treatment; let trained staff respond, and never press buttons or adjust the machine yourself.

lessons.title: Before leaving
lessons.body: Ask whether anything unusual happened during your session and confirm your next appointment. Stand up slowly. If you feel dizzy, weak or unwell, tell staff before you leave the chair. Make sure needle sites have stopped bleeding before you go, and know what to do if one starts bleeding at home. Arrange safe transport, especially if you often feel tired after treatment.

realSituation.title: Tatay Lito's quiet cramps
realSituation.body: Tatay Lito, 70, gets leg cramps in the last hour of every session but says nothing, not wanting to bother the busy nurses. One day he feels faint, and his blood pressure drops sharply.
realSituation.debrief: The nurse responds quickly and he recovers. Afterward, the team learns that his cramps had been a weekly warning that fluid was being removed faster than his body could adjust. They review his target weight, talk with him about salt and fluid between sessions, and ask him to report cramps the moment they begin. Speaking up early is part of the treatment, not a disturbance.

whatResearchShows.text: Symptoms during dialysis such as cramps and low blood pressure are common and are linked to rapid fluid removal. In DOPPS, shortening sessions and large weight gains between sessions were associated with worse outcomes. Early reporting allows staff to adjust treatment; this practice rests on clinical experience and guideline consensus.

modules.title: Protect fistulas, grafts and dialysis catheters
objectives: Identify your access type
Do the daily check your team taught you
Escalate access warning signs promptly
modules.everydayPicture: Your access is your lifeline, the doorway the dialysis machine uses to reach your blood. A fistula is your own artery joined directly to a vein, so the vein receives high-pressure, fast-flowing blood, grows thicker and becomes strong enough for needles. That fast flow is what you feel as a buzz, called a thrill, and hear as a whoosh. When the buzz changes or disappears, the flow may have slowed or stopped, and a clot can form within hours. That is why a quiet fistula is an urgent call, not a wait-and-see.

lessons.title: Name your access
lessons.body: Ask your team to show you which access you have: a fistula (artery joined to vein), a graft (a soft tube joining them), or a catheter (a tube in a large vein in the neck or chest, with two colored caps outside the skin). If you have a fistula or graft, learn to feel the thrill with your fingertips every morning and evening, and to listen if you were taught. If the buzz becomes weak, changes to a pulse-like beat, or disappears, contact your unit promptly; clots are often easier to clear when treated early.

lessons.title: Protect the access
lessons.body: Ask clinicians not to take blood pressure, draw blood or start drips on your access arm. Avoid tight sleeves, watches, bracelets and sleeping on that arm, and do not carry heavy bags hanging from it. Wear a medical bracelet or carry a card if you can. For catheters, keep the dressing clean, dry and covered as taught, and never open the caps or clamps. Protecting your access also means protecting the veins of your other arm for the future, so mention your kidney disease before any blood draw.

lessons.title: Have a bleeding plan
lessons.body: Bleeding from a needle site after dialysis is usually stopped with firm, steady pressure. Ask your nurse to show you exactly where and how to press, with clean gauze, and for how long before checking. Heavy or spurting bleeding that does not stop with pressure needs emergency help immediately: keep pressing while someone calls. Keep clean gauze and your contact card where you can find them quickly.

realSituation.title: The silent fistula
realSituation.body: On a Sunday morning, Kuya Dodong, 49, notices he cannot feel the usual buzz in his fistula. His next session is Monday, and he decides to wait.
realSituation.debrief: At Monday's session the nurse confirms no thrill: the fistula has clotted. Because nearly a day passed, the clot has hardened and the procedure to reopen it is more difficult; he needs a temporary catheter for a few weeks. His team explains that a call on Sunday morning could have led to an urgent assessment that day. Now he checks twice daily and has the unit's after-hours number saved on his phone.

whatResearchShows.text: Fistulas carry the lowest infection risk and catheters the highest, in CDC surveillance data (catheter risk about six times that of a fistula for Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection). The KDOQI 2019 guideline recommends patient education on access self-monitoring and early referral when an access changes, and emphasizes vein preservation.

modules.title: Use dialysis reviews to improve daily life
objectives: Prepare questions for your monthly or quarterly review
Report shortened or missed treatments and their causes
Choose one improvement to work on with the team
modules.everydayPicture: Your dialysis team reviews your care regularly using laboratory results, treatment records and what you tell them. Think of it like a jeepney's maintenance check: the mechanic reads the gauges, but only the driver knows that the engine shudders on uphill roads. Your experience of recovery time, sleep, appetite and energy is a gauge the laboratory cannot read.

lessons.title: A review looks beyond one number
lessons.body: Ask how your team measures whether dialysis is working: tests of how much waste is removed (such as Kt/V or URR, the urea reduction ratio), hemoglobin for anemia, potassium, phosphorus, calcium and parathyroid hormone for bones and heart, albumin for nutrition, and your blood pressure and weight. Then tell them what the numbers cannot: how long you need to recover after a session, whether you sleep, eat and itch, and which activities you are struggling to keep.

lessons.title: Talk about treatment time
lessons.body: Waste and potassium are removed steadily over the session, so cutting time short removes less. If transport, work, discomfort, childcare or cost makes it hard to finish your prescribed sessions, say so and ask for help solving the cause, such as a different shift, a transport schedule or symptom management. Never shorten or skip sessions on your own, even when you feel well.

lessons.title: Plan one improvement
lessons.body: Pick one problem to work on before the next review: post-dialysis fatigue, itching, transport, appetite or a laboratory result your team wants to improve. Agree on one action, who does it, and when you will check whether it helped. Small, tracked changes add up.

realSituation.body: Ate Joy, 44, a single mother, ends her sessions 30 minutes early twice a week to pick up her children from school. Her waste removal results begin to fall, and she feels more tired.
realSituation.debrief: At her review she explains the reason. The unit moves her to an earlier shift, and her sister agrees to fetch the children on two days. Her full sessions resume, her results recover over the following months, and she has more energy. The problem was never motivation; it was a schedule nobody had asked about.

whatResearchShows.text: In the international DOPPS study, skipping sessions was associated with about 30% higher mortality and shortening sessions was also linked with worse outcomes. Units with more highly trained staff hours had fewer patients skipping treatment. These are observational findings, but they support solving the causes of missed time together.

modules.title: Potassium, phosphorus and fluid between sessions: why the rules exist
objectives: Explain why potassium matters for the heart
Explain why phosphorus and binders matter for bones and blood vessels
Use your own plan to prepare for the longest gap between sessions
modules.everydayPicture: Between dialysis sessions, things you eat and drink build up in the blood like water rising behind a dam. On a three-times-a-week schedule, the gaps are not equal: the weekend gap is a full day longer, so the water rises highest just before the first session of the week. That is when potassium and fluid are most likely to reach dangerous levels, and when planning matters most.

lessons.title: Potassium and the heart
lessons.body: Potassium helps every muscle and nerve work, including the heart's electrical system. Healthy kidneys remove extra potassium every day; on dialysis, it accumulates between sessions. Too much can make the heartbeat irregular or even stop it, often with few warning signs except perhaps weakness or tingling. Whether you need to limit potassium, and how much, depends on your own blood results; many people on dialysis can still enjoy some fruits and vegetables with the right portions and preparation. Ask your dietitian, and be especially careful before the long weekend gap.

lessons.title: Phosphorus, binders and bones
lessons.body: Phosphorus is found in protein foods, dairy and especially in processed foods with phosphate additives, such as some processed meats, instant noodles and soft drinks. Dialysis removes only part of it. High phosphorus pulls calcium from bones and can deposit calcium in blood vessels and the heart, making them stiff. Phosphate binders are medicines that grab phosphorus in the food inside your gut, which is why they must be taken with meals, not on an empty stomach. Ask how to time yours with your actual meals and snacks.

lessons.title: Plan for the long gap
lessons.body: Look at your schedule and find your longest gap. Before it, follow your own plan for fluid, salt, potassium and phosphorus more carefully. Salty food makes you thirsty, so cutting salt is often the easiest way to drink less. Never skip the session after a long gap. If you feel unusual weakness, palpitations or breathlessness, seek urgent help.

realSituation.title: Christmas Eve and the long gap
realSituation.body: Tito Ernie, 62, dialyzes Monday, Wednesday and Friday. After his Friday session before Christmas, he enjoys Noche Buena: ham, fruit salad, buko juice and soft drinks. By Monday morning he feels weak and his legs feel heavy.
realSituation.debrief: The long weekend gap, potassium-rich buko juice and fruit, processed ham and extra fluid all piled up at once. At the unit his potassium is dangerously high, and the team treats it before and during dialysis. With his dietitian he plans next year's celebration: smaller portions, binders with the meal, less salty food, and a clear note of his own limits. He can still celebrate, just with a plan.

whatResearchShows.text: Large studies have found that deaths and hospitalizations among people on three-times-weekly hemodialysis cluster after the long interdialytic gap (observational data). In DOPPS, high phosphorus was associated with about 17% higher mortality. The KDOQI 2020 nutrition guideline recommends individualized potassium and phosphorus management guided by blood tests rather than blanket restrictions.

modules.title: Prepare for supervised peritoneal dialysis training
objectives: Describe how PD works in plain words
Prepare your home and helpers for training
Explain why only supervised training makes you ready
modules.everydayPicture: Your abdomen is lined by a thin, living membrane called the peritoneum, rich in tiny blood vessels. In peritoneal dialysis, a sterile fluid is drained into your belly through a soft tube. Waste moves from the blood vessels into the fluid, and a sugar in the fluid draws out extra water, the way salt draws water out of cucumbers when you make atchara. After some hours, the used fluid is drained out and replaced. The membrane does the filtering; your job, after training, is to keep every connection clean.

lessons.title: Learn what your pathway involves
lessons.body: PD is usually done at home. In continuous ambulatory PD (CAPD), you do several manual exchanges during the day. In automated PD (APD), a machine called a cycler does exchanges while you sleep. Both use a PD catheter placed in the abdomen by a surgeon or nephrologist, usually a few weeks before training. Your team will decide which form and equipment suit you. This lesson introduces PD; it does not teach you to perform exchanges.

lessons.title: Prepare the learning setting
lessons.body: Before training, think about your home: a clean, well-lit area for exchanges, a dry place off the floor for boxes of fluid, and a way to keep pets and dust away during connections. Tell the trainer about your eyesight, hand strength, memory, language and who will help you. PD can work well even in small homes and for people with limited help, but the trainer needs to know your situation to plan.

lessons.title: Practice with your trainer
lessons.body: A trained PD nurse teaches the exact steps for your equipment, watches you practice repeatedly and decides when you are ready. Training usually takes several days. Ask how to reach the PD team after hours, when your technique will be checked again, and who to call if a supply or machine problem happens. Watching a video or another patient is helpful background, but it is never a substitute for supervised practice.

realSituation.title: Learning from a cousin's video
realSituation.body: Bong, 38, a jeepney dispatcher, is scheduled for PD training next week. His cousin, also on PD, sends him videos and offers to teach him at home so he can "skip the training."
realSituation.debrief: Bong thanks his cousin but keeps the training appointment. His equipment differs from his cousin's, and the trainer corrects two steps in his technique that the videos had shown differently. He passes his practical assessment on day five, with his wife trained as his backup. The videos helped him arrive less nervous, but the training made him safe.

whatResearchShows.text: International PD training guidance (ISPD, 2025 position paper on teaching PD, abstract reviewed) emphasizes trainer preparation, hands-on practice, assessment and retraining. The ISPD 2022 peritonitis guideline also includes recommendations on PD training and reassessment as part of preventing infection.
