modules.title: Recognize PD infection and contamination concerns
objectives: Recognize cloudy drained fluid as urgent
Report a break in clean technique
Know the PD support and backup contacts
modules.everydayPicture: Used PD fluid should look clear enough that you could read a newspaper through the bag. When germs reach the peritoneum, white blood cells rush in to fight them, and the fluid turns cloudy, sometimes before pain or fever appear. That is why cloudy fluid is the earliest alarm of peritonitis, an infection of the abdominal lining. Treated early, most episodes clear with antibiotics; delayed, they can damage the membrane or end PD.

lessons.title: Know the warning signs
lessons.body: Cloudy drained fluid, abdominal pain or tenderness, fever, chills, nausea or vomiting can signal peritonitis. Redness, pain, swelling, crusting or pus at the catheter exit site can signal an exit-site infection, which can spread inward. Contact your PD team immediately for any of these, day or night, even if you feel fairly well. Keep the cloudy bag; the team will usually want it for testing.

lessons.title: Report a break in clean technique
lessons.body: If a connection touches something unclean, a cap falls off, a line cracks, or you are unsure whether a step was sterile, follow the response your trainer taught, and call the PD team promptly. Contamination does not always lead to infection, but reporting it lets the team decide whether you need preventive treatment. Never improvise a repair, and never add antibiotics or other medicines to a bag on your own.

lessons.title: Know the backup route
lessons.body: Keep the PD team's number and an after-hours or backup emergency contact on the wall near your exchange area and in your phone. If you are severely unwell, have severe abdominal pain, or cannot get urgent advice, go to the emergency department and bring your cloudy bag and your PD details. The clinical team directs tests, sample handling and treatment.

realSituation.title: Cloudy on a Saturday night
realSituation.body: Aling Merly, 61, on CAPD in Pampanga, sees a slightly cloudy bag at 10 p.m. on Saturday. Her belly feels only mildly sore, and she does not want to disturb the nurse on a weekend.
realSituation.debrief: Her daughter insists they call. The PD nurse asks them to bring the bag to the hospital that night; the fluid count confirms peritonitis, and antibiotics start before midnight. Merly recovers within days and stays on PD. Reviewing her technique, the trainer finds she had stopped wearing a mask during exchanges while she had a cold. Calling early protected both her health and her PD.

whatResearchShows.text: The ISPD 2022 peritonitis guideline recommends that PD programs keep overall peritonitis rates no higher than 0.40 episodes per patient-year at risk and that more than 80% of patients stay peritonitis-free each year. It also updates advice on managing contamination and on training and retraining. CDC guidance lists cloudy effluent, abdominal pain, fever and exit-site changes as signs to report.

modules.title: Organize home dialysis routines and reassessment
objectives: Keep the records your home team requests
Plan supplies, deliveries and backup help
Request retraining after any major change
modules.everydayPicture: Home dialysis gives freedom and responsibility in the same box. The unit staff are no longer in the room, so the home becomes a small clinic: supplies must arrive on time and stay dry, records must be kept, and skills must stay sharp. Skills fade quietly with time, illness and shortcuts, the way a driver who once passed the test can slowly pick up bad habits. Planned reassessment keeps the freedom safe.

lessons.title: Records help the home team
lessons.body: Keep the records your team asks for, using their forms and units, such as daily weight, blood pressure, the appearance of drained fluid, and how much fluid comes out. Bring them to every clinic visit. Report unusual findings according to your written action plan. Recording information does not authorize you to change your prescription; the team decides changes.

lessons.title: Make supplies manageable
lessons.body: Store boxes off the floor in a clean, dry, cool place, use the oldest stock first, and check bags for damage and expiry before use. Plan deliveries around holidays and typhoon season, and tell the team early about travel. Follow the unit's waste disposal instructions. Ask how to report damaged or questionable supplies, and never use a bag that looks wrong.

lessons.title: Ask for a skills review
lessons.body: Request reassessment after a hospital stay, an infection, a change in helper, new equipment, or whenever you feel unsure. Needing a refresher is a reason to ask, not a failure to hide. Note: if you are exploring home hemodialysis, this module covers only general home organization; home hemodialysis needs its own device-specific training through an authorized program.

realSituation.body: Tatay Nestor, 72, has done PD for three years with his wife's help. She is hospitalized, and his grandson Kevin, 22, offers to help after watching a few exchanges.
realSituation.debrief: Nestor calls the PD team, who schedule a training session for Kevin and a technique check for Nestor. The trainer notices Nestor has started skipping his hand-washing timer. Both receive a refresher; Kevin is assessed before helping alone. Three years of experience made Nestor confident, but the review made him safe again.

whatResearchShows.text: The ISPD 2022 peritonitis guideline recommends PD retraining after peritonitis, catheter infection, hospitalization, change in dexterity, vision or cognition, change in equipment, or interruption of PD. United States home dialysis regulations also require facility-based training and reassessment, which this course adapts as good practice rather than as Philippine law.

modules.title: Prepare for a kidney transplant evaluation
objectives: Describe transplant evaluation as a process
Prepare questions about living and deceased donation
Check costs and coordination early
modules.everydayPicture: A kidney transplant places a healthy kidney from a donor into the lower abdomen, where it is connected to blood vessels and the bladder; the old kidneys usually stay in place. The new kidney can do what dialysis cannot fully do: work all day, every day, including making hormones. But the body's immune system sees it as a stranger and will try to reject it unless medicines hold it back for as long as the kidney works. Evaluation is the process of checking whether the benefits outweigh those risks for you.

lessons.title: Ask about referral and evaluation
lessons.body: A transplant center evaluates your heart, blood vessels, infections, cancer screening, dental health, blood type and tissue matching, and also your support at home and your ability to take medicines every day. Some problems found during evaluation can be treated so you can proceed later. A referral or this course does not guarantee acceptance or a kidney. Ask what tests you need and how long the process usually takes at that center.

lessons.title: Donation needs independent safeguards
lessons.body: Kidneys can come from living donors, often relatives or spouses, or from deceased donors. A living donor receives their own separate evaluation and a team that looks after their interests, and can decline at any point without pressure. Buying or selling organs is illegal and harmful. If anyone offers a kidney for payment or pressures a relative to donate, tell the transplant team.

lessons.title: Coordinate the practical plan
lessons.body: Ask which appointments, laboratory tests and travel are needed, and who can accompany you. Ask a benefits coordinator to explain the applicable PhilHealth transplant package, what it covers, and separately, the costs of lifelong medicines and follow-up after transplant.

realSituation.title: Ana and her brother
realSituation.body: Ana, 31, on dialysis for a year, learns her brother Paolo wants to donate. Their mother pushes him hard, and Paolo privately feels unsure because he just got married.
realSituation.debrief: At the transplant center, Paolo meets his own donor team in a private appointment, where he can raise his doubts confidentially. He decides to proceed after counseling with his wife. Had he declined, the team would have told the family only that he was not a suitable donor, protecting his privacy. A good evaluation protects both the person receiving and the person giving.

whatResearchShows.text: In a landmark U.S. registry study of 228,552 people on dialysis, those who received a first deceased-donor transplant had a higher risk of death in the first weeks after surgery but a much lower long-term mortality, 48% to 82% lower than comparable people who stayed on the waiting list. Because selection matters, benefit is assessed individually by the transplant team.

modules.title: Build a safe routine after transplantation
objectives: Explain why every anti-rejection dose matters
Prepare a missed-dose and refill plan
Recognize follow-up and infection precautions as lifelong
modules.everydayPicture: Anti-rejection medicines work like a guard who keeps the immune system calm around the new kidney. The guard needs a steady level in the blood. Missed or late doses let the level fall, and the immune system can begin attacking quietly, often with no symptoms until damage shows in a blood test. Too much medicine, on the other hand, can harm the kidney and lower defenses against infection. That is why timing, consistency and blood level checks matter so much.

lessons.title: Protect the treatment plan
lessons.body: Take transplant medicines exactly as prescribed and at the same times every day; set alarms and use a pill organizer. Keep a current list and plan refills well before supplies run low, especially before holidays. Some foods and products, such as grapefruit and pomelo and certain herbal remedies, can change medicine levels; ask your transplant pharmacist before adding anything, including over-the-counter products.

lessons.title: Know how to get advice
lessons.body: Ask for written instructions now for a missed dose, vomiting soon after a dose, diarrhea, fever, or trouble getting medicines. Contact the transplant team promptly if a dose cannot be taken or kept down. Do not double, skip or stop doses on your own, and never switch brands without telling the team, since some generic versions require extra level checks.

lessons.title: Keep follow-up visible
lessons.body: Attend every blood test and clinic visit, even years later and even when you feel well; rejection is often silent. Report fever, pain over the transplant, less urine, swelling or sudden weight gain promptly. Ask about infection precautions, vaccines, sun protection, skin checks and safe food handling, because anti-rejection medicines lower your defenses.

realSituation.title: Rico's empty bottle
realSituation.body: Rico, 27, two years after transplant, runs out of one anti-rejection medicine during a long weekend in Baguio. Feeling fine, he decides to wait until Tuesday to refill.
realSituation.debrief: He remembers his transplant card and calls the team, who arrange an emergency supply at a nearby hospital pharmacy that night. His blood test the next week is stable. Afterward, he sets refill reminders two weeks ahead and keeps a three-day spare supply in his bag. Feeling fine was exactly why the gap was dangerous: rejection does not announce itself.

whatResearchShows.text: Nonadherence to anti-rejection medicine is a recognized cause of rejection and graft loss. A 2022 Cochrane review of 40 trials found that adherence interventions may improve dosing adherence, though evidence certainty was low; a 2025 meta-analysis of eight trials found that eHealth reminders and support improved adherence rates (risk ratio 1.19).

modules.title: Navigate transplant benefits across policy dates
objectives: Separate surgery coverage from post-transplant coverage

modules.everydayPicture: Transplant coverage comes in chapters: evaluation, surgery for the recipient and donor, and years of follow-up and medicines. Each chapter can be governed by a different circular, and circulars are revised. Reading only the headline is like reading only the cover of a book: you know the title but not the story.

lessons.title: Different phases have different policies
lessons.body: Ask the coordinator to explain coverage for evaluation, transplant surgery, donor care and ongoing post-transplant services separately. Do not assume the surgical package covers lifelong medicines. Adult and pediatric post-transplant services are covered by separate circulars (PhilHealth Circulars 2025-0012 and 2025-0011), and eligibility conditions apply.

lessons.title: Check the transition
lessons.body: PhilHealth published Circular 2026-0019, revising the transplant package, on November 21, 2026. Its effectivity clause gives an expected effective date of December 6, 2026, fifteen days after publication; this date was calculated from the clause, not confirmed operationally. The circular also keeps the earlier rules for procedures pre-authorized and performed under the previous policy. Ask the coordinator which policy applies to your case and from what date.

lessons.title: Confirm your own estimate
lessons.body: Ask for a dated, written explanation of the applicable package, your eligibility, whether the hospital is contracted, and any charges you may need to pay. An advertised top rate is not a promise of personal coverage.

realSituation.debrief: The benefits coordinator checks the circular's transition section and explains which rules apply to a case pre-authorized under the earlier policy, gives the family a dated written estimate, and separates the surgery estimate from post-transplant medicine costs. modules.title: Understand conservative kidney management
objectives: Describe conservative kidney management as active care
Prepare a goals conversation
Identify your ongoing care contacts
modules.everydayPicture: For some people, especially those who are older or living with several serious illnesses, dialysis may add burden without adding much good time. Conservative kidney management (CKM) is the choice to focus fully on comfort, function and what matters most, without dialysis. It is not "doing nothing." Think of it as changing the destination of the trip from "as many kilometers as possible" to "the best journey possible," with the same skilled driver still at the wheel.

lessons.title: Care continues
lessons.body: CKM includes protecting remaining kidney function with medicines and diet, treating anemia, controlling fluid and blood pressure, and managing symptoms such as itch, breathlessness, poor sleep, nausea and pain. It includes emotional, spiritual and family support, and planning for the future. Ask your kidney team how they would address your own needs and who would coordinate your care.

lessons.title: Discuss benefits and burdens honestly
lessons.body: Talk about what matters most to you, what dialysis would involve for you, such as travel three times a week, hospital stays and access procedures, and what is uncertain. For some older adults with many illnesses, dialysis may extend life only modestly while increasing time in hospital. For others, it adds meaningful time. Include a supporter if you wish, and ask how the plan can be revisited.

lessons.title: Leave with support
lessons.body: Ask who manages your symptoms, how to reach the team, and what to do if your condition changes suddenly. Ask whether home visits, palliative care or hospice services are available near you. Choosing CKM should never leave you without medical and emotional support, and you may change your mind.

realSituation.title: Lola Iska's priority
realSituation.body: Lola Iska, 86, with dementia and heart failure, has kidney function at about one-tenth of normal. Her children disagree: one wants dialysis "to do everything," another fears it would mean spending her last months in hospital.
realSituation.debrief: The kidney team meets the family, explains the likely benefits and burdens for someone in Lola Iska's situation, and asks what Lola herself had valued. She had always said she wanted to stay home. The family chooses CKM with home visits, medicines for breathlessness and itch, and a plan for her final weeks. Her children say later that they felt they had done everything that mattered.

whatResearchShows.text: A 2025 Cochrane review comparing CKM with dialysis in older people found no randomized trials. Observational studies suggested lower survival with CKM on average, but the evidence was very low certainty because sicker people more often chose CKM; quality-of-life differences were small and uncertain. A 2026 review concluded that dialysis survival gains shrink with frailty and multimorbidity, and that people choosing CKM were more likely to die at home.

askYourTeam: For someone in my situation, what might dialysis add, and what might it cost me in time and comfort?
What would conservative kidney management include for me?
Who will look after my symptoms, and how do I reach them?
modules.activity: On W19, write two goals and two questions for a kidney supportive care appointment.
modules.teachBack: Explain why conservative management still needs an active clinical plan.

quiz.stem: What does conservative kidney management mean?

options.text: An online instruction to stop current treatment
Active symptom and quality-of-life care without dialysis or transplantation
No medical care or symptom support

quiz.rationale: It is a planned care approach discussed with the treating team.

quiz.stem: After choosing CKM, can a person change their mind?

options.text: No, the choice is final
Yes, plans can be revisited with the team
Only with a court order

quiz.rationale: Goals change, and the plan can be reviewed.

quiz.stem: How certain is the evidence comparing CKM with dialysis in older adults?

options.text: Very certain, from many randomized trials
Uncertain, mainly from observational studies
There is no evidence at all

quiz.rationale: No randomized trials exist; observational evidence is very low certainty, so individual discussion is essential.

modules.title: Plan for comfort and future care conversations
objectives: Track your symptom priorities
Choose who joins a future-care discussion
Ask how your preferences can be documented
modules.everydayPicture: Families often say the hardest moments came when no one knew what their loved one would have wanted. Talking about future care while you can speak for yourself is a gift to the people who may one day decide for you. It is not giving up; it is making sure your voice is still heard when you cannot raise it.

lessons.title: Start with today
lessons.body: Tell your team which symptoms most affect your comfort and daily life, such as itching, pain, breathlessness, poor sleep, nausea, low mood or worry. Many can be eased. Your support plan can include physical, emotional, family, financial and spiritual needs; ask about a chaplain, priest, pastor or imam if faith matters to you.

lessons.title: Talk about future situations
lessons.body: If you wish, discuss who should speak for you if you cannot communicate, what you would want if you became very ill, and what matters most: being at home, being free of pain, being with family, or trying every treatment. Ask a clinician how these preferences can be documented in your setting, since forms and legal recognition vary.

lessons.title: Make the plan usable
lessons.body: Share your preferences with the people you choose and keep a copy where it can be found. Ask who reviews the plan and how to get help outside regular hours. This course does not create legally binding advance directives or do-not-resuscitate orders; those require your clinical team and the applicable local process.

realSituation.title: Manang Elsa's kitchen-table talk
realSituation.body: Manang Elsa, 78, on dialysis for six years, tells her nurse she is tired of hospital stays and worries her children will fight if she can no longer speak.
realSituation.debrief: The nurse arranges a family meeting with her nephrologist. Elsa names her eldest daughter to speak for her, says she wants to avoid a breathing machine but continue dialysis while it helps her feel well, and asks for her priest to visit. The team documents her wishes using the hospital's process. Months later, when Elsa becomes very ill, her children follow her words without conflict.

whatResearchShows.text: Advance care planning and kidney supportive care are recommended by international kidney and palliative care groups, and NIDDK patient guidance describes symptom-focused care and future planning as active parts of kidney care. Evidence comes mainly from observational studies and qualitative research about patient and family experience.

askYourTeam: Which of my symptoms can be eased, and how?
How can my wishes about future care be written down here?
Can my family join a meeting with you?
modules.activity: Use W19 to draft a conversation invitation and a symptom priority; take formal documentation questions to the care team.
modules.teachBack: Explain who can help turn your preferences into locally appropriate documentation.

quiz.stem: Where should formal treatment-limitation decisions be made and recorded?

options.text: With the responsible clinical team through the applicable local process
Automatically in the course completion form
By a care partner without involving a capable patient

quiz.rationale: Educational reflection does not create a medical order or replace consent.

quiz.stem: Why talk about future care while you are well enough to speak?

options.text: So your wishes guide decisions if you cannot speak later
Because it ends your current treatment
It has no benefit

quiz.rationale: Early conversations let your voice guide care and reduce family conflict.

quiz.stem: Which needs can a supportive care plan include?

options.text: Only physical symptoms
Physical, emotional, family, financial and spiritual needs
Only financial needs

quiz.rationale: Supportive care addresses the whole person and family.

modules.title: Support someone while protecting their choices
objectives: Agree on a support role with the person you help
Ask before sharing information
Recognize the limits of informal support
modules.everydayPicture: Filipino families care deeply, and that love sometimes turns into taking over: answering for the patient, deciding meals, hiding bad news. Good support is more like being a co-pilot than a driver. The co-pilot reads the map, watches the road and offers help, but the driver, if able, keeps the wheel. People who keep control over their own care tend to stay more engaged in it.

lessons.title: Ask what help is wanted
lessons.body: Begin with the person's preferences. They may want help taking notes, arranging transport, remembering appointments or cooking, while wanting to manage their medicines themselves. Agree which tasks you will do and which they will keep. Revisit the agreement when health or circumstances change.

lessons.title: Support the conversation
lessons.body: Ask permission before joining a consultation, and help prepare questions beforehand. In the room, let the person speak first and fill gaps only when invited. Check what information they agree may be shared, and with whom; being family does not automatically give you access to their records. If they lose the ability to decide, the team will guide you on the proper process.

lessons.title: Keep clinical boundaries clear
lessons.body: Helping with daily life does not authorize clinical procedures. PD exchanges, catheter care and similar tasks require training and assessment by the home team, and some tasks belong only to professionals. Ask for help when a task goes beyond your agreed role or your comfort.

realSituation.title: Who answers the doctor?
realSituation.body: At every visit, Marites answers all the doctor's questions for her father, Mang Andoy, 70, who is fully able to speak for himself. He grows quiet and stops mentioning his own worries.
realSituation.debrief: The nurse gently asks to hear from Mang Andoy first. He reveals he has been skipping a medicine because it makes him urinate at night during jeepney trips. Marites had never known. They agree that he speaks first, and she takes notes. His medicine timing is changed. Support that preserves his voice uncovered a problem that support that replaced it had hidden.

whatResearchShows.text: A systematic review of caregivers of adults on maintenance dialysis (61 studies, 5,367 caregivers) found that caregivers' quality of life is poorer than the general population's. A 2026 mixed-methods review found that education and empowerment-based support for family caregivers improved caregiver quality of life, anxiety, depression and confidence, with mixed effects on burden.

askYourTeam: (Asked together) Which tasks would you like help with, and which do you want to keep?
How can I be told about updates, with the patient's agreement?
Which tasks require training before I help?
modules.activity: On W20, write a shared support agreement with three agreed tasks and one boundary; the patient may decline participation.
modules.teachBack: Explain how you would respond if you and the patient prefer different plans.

quiz.stem: A capable patient wants to answer for themselves. What should a care partner do?

options.text: Answer every question over them
Treat course completion as authority to decide
Support their choice and offer help if requested

quiz.rationale: Support should preserve the patient's participation and choices.

quiz.stem: Does being a family member give you automatic access to the patient's records?

options.text: Yes
No; a capable patient decides what is shared
Only if you live together

quiz.rationale: Health information is private; access follows the patient's consent.

quiz.stem: The patient asks you to do their PD exchange tonight, but you have never been trained. What should you do?

options.text: Try it carefully
Contact the PD team for guidance and arrange training before helping
Watch a video and proceed

quiz.rationale: Clinical tasks require training and assessment by the home team.

modules.title: Organize appointments, records and practical support
objectives: Create a shared task plan
Give a clear handoff when calling a service
Protect private information in family communication
modules.everydayPicture: Kidney care generates a surprising amount of logistics: three sessions a week, laboratory schedules, refills, PhilHealth papers, transport and meals. When it lives only in one person's head, everything collapses the day that person gets sick. A shared plan works like a family relay race: everyone knows their leg and where the baton is.

lessons.title: Make tasks visible
lessons.body: Agree who helps with appointments, transport, meals, refills and paperwork. Use a simple shared calendar, on paper on the refrigerator or on a phone, and name a backup for each key task. Avoid assuming one person can be available all the time; overseas relatives can help with scheduling, reminders or costs even from afar.

lessons.title: Hand over facts
lessons.body: When calling a service, state your name and role, whether the patient has agreed to your involvement, the concern, when it started and what you observed. Ask who will respond, by when, and what to do if things worsen. Write down the name of the person you spoke with.

lessons.title: Share carefully
lessons.body: Keep documents in an agreed place and use private channels for medical information. Avoid posting prescriptions, laboratory results, PhilHealth numbers or photos of records in large family group chats or on social media, where they can spread beyond your control. Ask the facility how authorized supporters can receive updates.

realSituation.title: The family group chat
realSituation.body: The Santos family coordinates Lolo Ben's dialysis in a 60-member group chat, where someone posts his laboratory results and PhilHealth details. Meanwhile, nobody is sure who is driving him on Friday.
realSituation.debrief: His granddaughter sets up a small private chat for the four people who actually help, with a weekly roster and a named backup driver, and asks the family to delete the posted documents. Lolo Ben agrees which updates the wider family gets. Fewer people, clearer jobs, safer information.

whatResearchShows.text: Health information is sensitive personal information under the Philippine Data Privacy Act (Republic Act 10173). Caregiver support programs that include practical organization and education are associated with better caregiver confidence (2026 systematic review).

askYourTeam: How can authorized family members receive updates?
Whom do we call to change an appointment or transport?
Which documents should we keep at home?
modules.activity: On W21, make a fictional one-week support roster and rehearse handing over an appointment change.
modules.teachBack: Explain how a backup helper gets the information they are authorized to receive.

quiz.stem: Which record belongs in an open public group chat?

options.text: The patient's membership number and prescriptions
None; use an agreed private channel for medical information
A photo of the full medical record

quiz.rationale: Practical coordination should not expose private medical information.

quiz.stem: When you call the dialysis unit for a patient, what should you say first?

options.text: Your name, your role and whether the patient agreed to your involvement
Only the patient's complaint
Nothing until they ask

quiz.rationale: Clear identification and consent help the service respond appropriately.

quiz.stem: Why name a backup for each key task?

options.text: So care continues when the usual helper is unavailable
To share the blame
It is not needed

quiz.rationale: A plan that depends on one person fails when that person is sick or away.

practicalEvidence.prompt: Explain how a backup helper gets the information they are authorized to receive.

modules.title: Prevent care partner burnout and arrange backup
objectives: Recognize signs of overload in yourself
Ask for specific help
Plan respite and safe backup
modules.everydayPicture: Caring for someone with kidney failure is often a marathon run at sprint speed. Many care partners, especially wives and daughters, keep going until their own health breaks. An empty cup cannot pour. Looking after yourself is not selfish; it keeps the care going.

lessons.title: Notice your own limits
lessons.body: Warning signs include poor sleep, irritability, frequent illness, skipped medical checkups of your own, missed work and withdrawing from friends. Feeling guilt, resentment or sadness is common and human. Tell the care team when the current arrangement is no longer workable; they would rather adjust the plan than lose you.

lessons.title: Ask for a concrete task
lessons.body: "Can someone help?" rarely works. "Can you drive Tatay to dialysis every Wednesday this month?" usually does. List tasks others could take, and match them to people's real abilities. A social worker, parish group or patient organization may know of local support. Availability and cost of respite vary.

lessons.title: Make backup safe
lessons.body: A replacement helper needs the right information and, for clinical home treatment tasks, training and assessment by the home team. Tell the treatment team about a gap in support before a treatment is missed, not after.

realSituation.title: Ate Rowena's breaking point
realSituation.body: Ate Rowena, 46, has cared alone for her husband on PD for two years while working part-time. She has stopped seeing friends, sleeps four hours a night, and one morning forgets a step during an exchange.
realSituation.debrief: She tells the PD nurse, who arranges retraining and suggests her brother-in-law also be trained as backup. A social worker connects her with a parish support group, and she schedules one free evening a week. Her husband had not realized how exhausted she was. Asking early protected both of them.

whatResearchShows.text: Caregiver quality of life is poorer than the general population's and comparable to caregivers for other chronic diseases (systematic review, 61 studies). Educational and psychosocial support for caregivers of people on hemodialysis improved caregiver quality of life, anxiety and depression in a 2026 review, although effects on burden were mixed.

askYourTeam: What support is available for care partners here?
Can a second person be trained as backup?
Whom do I tell if I can no longer manage?
modules.activity: On W21, identify one task to delegate and one backup arrangement; ask the team what training a substitute would need.
modules.teachBack: Practice requesting a specific period of help without promising untrained dialysis coverage.

quiz.stem: You cannot continue helping with a trained home dialysis task tomorrow. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the home team promptly and arrange an appropriately trained backup plan
Send any available relative without training
Hide the problem until treatment is missed

quiz.rationale: Support continuity and clinical task competence need coordinated planning.

quiz.stem: Which request is most likely to get real help?

options.text: "Can someone help sometime?"
"Can you drive Tatay to dialysis every Wednesday this month?"
Posting that you are tired

quiz.rationale: Specific, time-bound requests are easier to say yes to.

quiz.stem: Is taking regular rest as a care partner selfish?

options.text: Yes
No; it helps you keep caring safely
Only if the patient complains

quiz.rationale: Care partner wellbeing sustains the care.

modules.title: Support children, teens and growing independence
objectives: Ask for age-appropriate teaching from the pediatric team
Plan school communication
Arrange a transition discussion for teenagers
modules.everydayPicture: Children are not small adults. Their kidneys, bones and brains are still growing, their medicines are dosed by weight, and kidney disease can affect growth, schooling and friendships. Adolescence adds another layer: the move from parents managing care to the young person managing it, often just as they are testing independence in every other part of life.

lessons.title: Children need their own care plan
lessons.body: A child's kidney care, medicines, nutrition and development need pediatric kidney expertise. Never use an adult target, food limit or dose for a child. Ask the pediatric team to explain, in age-appropriate words, what the child can understand and safely do, and how to watch for growth and developmental concerns.

lessons.title: Include the young person
lessons.body: Use simple, honest explanations and invite questions. Agree with the family, the young person and the team what the school should know, such as medicine times, toilet access, activity limits and emergency contacts. Ask about play, sports, attendance and emotional support, including how siblings are coping.

lessons.title: Prepare for growing independence
lessons.body: Start gradually in early adolescence: letting the teen speak first in visits, learn their medicines, and book a refill. Ask who coordinates the move to adult services, what skills will be practiced, and when the first joint visit will be. This module is family orientation, not a complete pediatric curriculum.

realSituation.title: JM turns seventeen
realSituation.body: JM, 17, received a kidney transplant at 12. His mother has always managed his medicines. Now in senior high school, he wants freedom, stays out late, and sometimes skips evening doses.
realSituation.debrief: The pediatric team meets JM alone first, then with his mother. They set up phone alarms, a plan for him to fill his own pill box with his mother checking weekly, and a first visit to the adult transplant clinic with his pediatric nurse present. His blood levels stabilize. Handing over responsibility gradually, with a safety net, protected both his kidney and his independence.

whatResearchShows.text: Adolescents and young adults have the highest kidney transplant failure rates of any age group, with adherence and the transfer from pediatric to adult care as major contributors. Structured, developmentally appropriate transition programs are recommended, and evidence supports their benefits (reviews, 2022 and 2023).

askYourTeam: What can my child learn to do at this age?
What should we tell the school, and who should tell them?
When and how will my teenager move to adult kidney care?
modules.activity: On W22, prepare a school or transition conversation with no treatment targets; involve the pediatric service.
modules.teachBack: Explain why adult advice cannot simply be scaled down for a child.

quiz.stem: Which plan should determine a child's medicines and nutrition?

options.text: The adult course targets divided by two
Advice copied from another adult patient
The child's pediatric kidney team plan

quiz.rationale: Pediatric needs require individualized specialist assessment.

quiz.stem: Which age group has the highest kidney transplant failure rates?

options.text: Adolescents and young adults
Young children
Middle-aged adults

quiz.rationale: Adherence challenges and the transfer to adult care contribute; planned transition helps.

quiz.stem: What is a good first step toward a teenager's independence in kidney care?

options.text: Hand over everything at once on their 18th birthday
Let them speak first in visits and learn their medicines gradually
Keep them out of all discussions

quiz.rationale: Gradual, supported handover builds skills safely.

modules.title: Recover after hospital care and rebuild your plan
objectives: Reconcile discharge instructions with your usual plan
Make sure the discharge plan reaches your kidney team
Request support or retraining after a major change
modules.everydayPicture: Leaving the hospital is a handoff between teams, and handoffs are where dropped balls happen. A medicine stopped in the ward may still be in your box at home; a new medicine may duplicate an old one under a different brand name; your dialysis unit may not know you were admitted. The first week home is when these gaps cause harm, so it deserves a deliberate check.

lessons.title: Check what changed
lessons.body: Before leaving, ask the ward team to go through every medicine: what is new, what stopped, what changed dose, and why. At home, compare the discharge list with your old list and your actual medicine box. Bring both lists to your kidney team or pharmacist so differences are resolved. Do not combine conflicting instructions on your own.

lessons.title: Make the handoff reach the right team
lessons.body: Ask how your dialysis unit, kidney doctor and primary care doctor will receive the discharge summary, and bring a copy to your next session or visit. If you are on dialysis, tell the unit your target weight may have changed during illness. Know whom to call about an unclear instruction, and report new or worsening symptoms through the agreed route.

lessons.title: Review support and skills
lessons.body: Illness can change strength, memory, appetite and the help you need. Ask about rehabilitation, nutrition support, home help or retraining for PD or other home tasks. Update your learning path and your care partner arrangements after any big change.

realSituation.title: Two lists, one patient
realSituation.body: Mang Jose, 68, on hemodialysis, is discharged after pneumonia with a new list. At home his old box still holds a blood pressure medicine the ward had stopped because his pressure was low, and a new brand that is actually the same drug as one he already takes.
realSituation.debrief: His daughter brings both lists and the medicine box to his next dialysis session. The nurse and nephrologist spot the duplicate and the stopped medicine, reconcile the list, and lower his target weight, which had changed during the illness. One deliberate check prevented a likely fall in blood pressure during dialysis.

whatResearchShows.text: Hospital stays with acute kidney injury are followed by higher long-term risks of death, dialysis and CKD (2026 meta-analysis), and a qualitative study found that many survivors were not told about their kidney injury or how to manage it at home. Medication reconciliation at transitions is standard safety practice.

askYourTeam: What changed in my medicines, and why?
Has my target weight or dialysis plan changed?
Do I need rehabilitation or retraining after this illness?

modules.teachBack: Explain what you would do if hospital and dialysis instructions conflict.

quiz.stem: Two discharge lists give different directions. What is the next step?

options.text: Follow both lists at the same time
Ask the responsible clinical team or pharmacist to reconcile them promptly
Choose the higher dose yourself

quiz.rationale: Conflicting instructions require a clear, reconciled plan.

quiz.stem: Why should your dialysis unit know about a recent hospital stay?

options.text: Your medicines and target weight may have changed
Only for billing
It does not matter

quiz.rationale: Illness often changes medicines and body weight, which affects dialysis.

quiz.stem: What should you bring to your first visit after discharge?

options.text: The discharge summary, both medicine lists and your medicine box
Nothing
Only your PhilHealth card

quiz.rationale: These let the team find and fix discrepancies.
